seoTitle: How to Reset TradingView Settings and Chart Style to Default
metaDescription: Cluttered charts or custom indicators taking over your view? Learn how to restore TradingView's default candlestick style, timeframes, and layout.
intro: If custom indicators, drawings, or color tweaks have left your TradingView chart looking nothing like the clean layout you started with, you don't need to rebuild it from scratch — TradingView has dedicated commands for wiping a chart back to its defaults. This guide covers the right-click reset menu that clears drawings and indicators in one move, the Settings panel where candle body, border, and wick colors actually live, and the timezone setting that's easy to overlook but changes how every candle on your chart lines up with the clock.

steps.heading: Start from your current chart so you know what's changed
steps.body: Before resetting anything, take a look at your chart as it currently sits — indicator panels stacked under the price action, an EMA and SMA line overlaid on the candles, and the watchlist docked on the right showing your other tracked symbols. Knowing what's actually on the chart (which indicators, which drawings) makes it easier to decide whether you want a full reset or just to strip back a few specific additions.

image.caption: A working TradingView chart with EMA and SMA lines applied, a live watchlist docked on the right, and the standard toolbar running along the top.

steps.heading: Right-click the chart for the reset menu
steps.body: Right-clicking anywhere on the chart canvas opens a context menu with the commands that matter most for a cleanup: Reset chart view at the top, and further down, Remove drawings and Remove indicators, each listing the exact count currently applied — "Remove 6 drawings," "Remove 3 indicators," for example. Reset chart view snaps the zoom and scroll position back to default without touching your indicators or drawings, so use it first if the chart just looks zoomed or scrolled oddly rather than visually cluttered.

image.caption: The right-click context menu, showing Reset chart view at the top and, further down, options to remove all current drawings or all current indicators with their exact counts listed.

steps.heading: Clear indicators and drawings from that same menu
steps.body: Click Remove indicators to strip every indicator currently applied to the chart in one action, and Remove drawings to clear any trendlines, shapes, or annotations you've added. Both commands only affect the active chart, not your saved layouts or any indicators you've purchased or added to your account library — they're still available to reapply any time from the indicators panel. This is the fastest way back to a bare price chart when things have piled up over weeks of analysis.

steps.heading: Reset the candlestick style in Settings
steps.body: Open Settings and go to the Canvas tab, which is where candle appearance actually lives — separate checkboxes for Body, Borders, and Wick, each with its own up/down color swatches, plus a "Color bars based on previous close" option that changes how TradingView decides whether a candle counts as up or down. If your candles have been recolored or resized from a template you applied earlier, this is the panel to fix it in — toggle the boxes back on and set the color swatches to TradingView's standard green and red.

image.caption: The Settings panel's Canvas tab, with Candles options for Body, Borders, and Wick colors, and a Data modification section covering Precision and Timezone.

steps.heading: Check precision and timezone in the same panel
steps.body: Below the candle color options, the same Canvas tab holds Data modification settings for Precision and Timezone. Precision controls how many decimal places prices display with — leave it on Default unless you're trading an asset that needs more granularity. Timezone is worth double-checking specifically, since a chart set to the wrong region will still look visually correct but report candle open and close times that don't match your local clock, which throws off session-based analysis.

steps.heading: Reapply a template or save your reset as the new default
steps.body: Once the chart looks the way you want, the Template dropdown at the bottom of the Settings panel lets you save this configuration so new charts open with it automatically, instead of inheriting whatever customizations you had before. If you'd rather keep experimenting without committing, just click Cancel or Ok without saving a template — your reset still applies to the current chart either way, it just won't carry forward to new ones.

faq.question: Can I reset TradingView settings without losing my saved layouts?
faq.answer: Yes. Removing indicators and drawings from the right-click menu, or resetting candle colors in Settings, only affects the chart you're currently viewing — other saved layouts are untouched unless you separately open and reset them.

faq.question: Does resetting TradingView settings work the same on mobile?
faq.answer: The core commands — resetting the chart view and clearing indicators or drawings — are available on both desktop and mobile, though the menus you tap through to reach them differ slightly by platform.

faq.question: Will resetting my chart remove indicators I paid for?
faq.answer: No. Removing indicators from a chart only clears them from that chart's current view — it doesn't remove your access to any indicator you've purchased or added to your account, and you can reapply it any time.

faq.question: Why would I want to reset TradingView to its default settings?
faq.answer: A reset clears away clutter built up from applying indicators, drawings, and color tweaks over time, giving you a simpler, more focused chart — useful both for a fresh start and for troubleshooting when a chart is displaying something unexpected.

faq.question: Where do I change the candlestick colors specifically?
faq.answer: Open Settings and go to the Canvas tab. The Candles section there has separate color controls for Body, Borders, and Wick, each with an up-candle and down-candle swatch.
